message.content:
Below is a concise summary of key tenant‑rights protections under Texas law (Texas Property Code). This is general information and **not** legal advice; if you have a specific dispute or question, consult a licensed attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What the law says | Practical take‑away | |------|-------------------|---------------------| | **Security Deposit Limits** | A landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a non‑furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for a furnished unit. | Keep records of the amount paid and the receipt. | | **Deposit Return** | Landlord must return the deposit within **30 days after the lease ends**, unless they provide a written itemized list of deductions. | Ask for the itemization in writing if you’re told money will be withheld. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: landlord must give at least **30 days’ notice** before the lease expires if they intend to raise rent or change terms. | If you receive a notice to vacate, check whether it meets the required time frame. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | Under §92.001–92.006, landlords must keep premises safe, sanitary, and fit for habitation (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural integrity). | Report needed repairs in writing; if the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (but follow proper procedure). | | **Rent Increases** | No statutory limit on how much a landlord can increase rent, but increases must be in writing and given **at least 90 days’ notice** for a lease renewal. | Verify that any rent increase notice complies with this timeline. | | **Eviction Process** | Landlords must serve a written notice (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for other reasons) and file an unlawful detainer action in court. | If served a notice, respond promptly; failure to do so can lead to a judgment against you. | | **Discrimination Protections** | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Act, discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap is prohibited. | If you suspect discrimination, document all interactions and consider filing a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Attorney General. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or others. | If the landlord repeatedly enters without notice or causes disturbances, you may seek a restraining order or damages. | | **Lease Modification** | Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | Do not sign a new agreement until you read and agree to all terms. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document everything** – keep copies of receipts, emails, text messages, and photos of conditions. 2. **Get notices in writing** – verbal notices are harder to enforce. 3. **Know your timeline** – many actions require advance written notice (rent increase, termination, entry). 4. **Use official forms** – e.g., the Texas “Notice to Pay Rent or Quit” (Form 13‑201) is available online. 5. **Seek help early** – contact local tenant‑rights groups, the Texas Attorney General’s Office, or a qualified attorney if you face a dispute. #### Useful Resources | Resource | Link | |----------|------| | Texas Attorney General – Tenant Rights | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/housing | | HUD – Fair Housing Complaint | https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/fair_housing_equal_opp/complaint | | Texas Legal Services Center – Free legal aid | https://texaslegalservices.org/ | | Texas Tenants Association (non‑profit advocacy) | https://www.tentexas.org/ | --- If you’re dealing with a specific issue—such as a disputed security deposit, a notice to quit, or alleged discrimination—please let me know the details (without personal identifying data), and I can point you toward the relevant statutes or suggest next steps.
